source.title: Towards Engineering Scaling Laws with Pretraining Data Composition
source.authors: Jan-Lucas Uslu; K. Greif; D. Whiteson; B. Nachman

record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling behavior in a new domain and training regime: jet classification models pretrained on different data compositions and fine-tuned on a downstream task.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own compute-optimal scaling exponents and downstream test-loss comparisons for jet classifiers. These bear on allocation trends and scaling beyond text, but are not results about language-model pretraining loss. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP (Approach 2) and parametric-fit (Approach 3) scaling analysis. It covers a new domain and regime: transformer jet classifiers (3K–10.5M params) fine-tuned on JetClass after different pretraining corpora, or trained from scratch. It reports compute-optimal exponents for N* and D*. This bears on V5 (power-law form beyond text, including fine-tuning/transfer) and V7 (exponents depend on data composition and fitting method). It is not a language-model study, so V3's LM allocation claim and V1/V2/V6 are not directly tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that pretraining composition reshapes compute-optimal scaling for jet classification. QCD-only pretraining lowers loss but roughly keeps scratch exponents (a≈b≈0.5). Adding BSM resonance jets shifts the split toward data (a≈0.22, b≈0.78). They claim the shift is robust across both extraction methods. They note that diversity and alignment are not separated and that generalization to other tasks and larger scales is unverified.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Hoffmann-style IsoFLOP-profile and parametric-fit approaches to estimate compute-optimal scaling, but applies them to jet-classification fine-tuning after physics-data pretraining rather than language-model pretraining. The study also varies pretraining-data composition.
record.method_sensitivity: Pretraining subset composition changes the fitted exponents. The two extraction approaches give similar but offset values for BSM-containing subsets; parametric loss-surface fit quality is reported as poor.

fits_no_version.finding: Pretraining (QCD-only and especially BSM-augmented) lowers downstream fine-tuning loss vs scratch at all model sizes, with a larger benefit for larger models (Fig. 3, figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transfer benefit from pretraining grows with model size, and its size depends on pretraining-downstream alignment.

record.problems: The authors report poor fit quality for the parametric loss-surface approach and suspect more runs, especially for larger models, could improve it. They say the small statistics and variance in minimum test loss leave open whether the poor fit reflects noise or a true departure from the assumed form. The study tests one pretraining setup and one fine-tuning task, does not separate diversity from downstream alignment, and says generalization to larger scales remains unverified.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying result rows were omitted. Absolute loss curves and loss contours are shown in figures without numerical values; the explicit textual comparisons are recorded in R21–R24. Prior-study results cited in Related Work were excluded.

untested.parts: All: no language-model pretraining loss. No loss-vs-N/D/C exponents are reported even for jets.
All: no extrapolation from small fits to much larger runs.
All for language models. The jet-domain allocation results are recorded under V5/V7. The scratch result (a≈b≈0.5) merely echoes the Hoffmann allocation in another domain.
All: depth fixed at 4; shape not varied at fixed N.
Image/video, repeated-data regimes, other physics tasks, and scales beyond 10.5M params. Pretraining compute is fixed, so pretraining-scale scaling is untested.
All: no downstream-task predictability from scale or pretraining loss is measured.
Parameter counting, training schedule, and curve bending away from a single power law at larger scale.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not one of the original sources. V3 links were removed because the system is a jet classifier, not a language model; the allocation results count under V5 (fine-tuning/transfer regime) and V7. Three caveats: (1) The authors' robustness claim glosses over the QCD-only case, where the parametric fit gives a=0.425 vs 0.526; under that method QCD-only pretraining would also shift the split. (2) The Fig. 1 caption claims 'good agreement' of the parametric fit with IsoFLOP slices, while the text and Appendix call the fit poor. (3) Scale is small (≤10.5M params, C≈1e12–1e16), the sweep has 12 sizes × 5 seeds, and uncertainties come only from test-set bootstrap, not seed or fit variation. The α and β of the parametric fit are not reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out pretraining loss in language models, or power-law loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute when the other factors are not bottlenecks.
No small-run fits are used to predict the loss of runs orders of magnitude larger.

Tests compute-optimal model-size and dataset-size scaling for jet-classification fine-tuning, not language-model parameter and training-token allocations. It does not test the specific Kaplan-versus-Hoffmann comparison in language models.
Depth is fixed at 4 layers; the study does not vary architecture details at fixed parameter count.

Tests jet-classification models with a particular pretraining and fine-tuning setup. It does not test image/video models, repeated-data regimes, or generalization across other tasks and larger scales.
Reports downstream jet-classification test loss across model sizes and pretraining conditions, but does not test downstream language-model tasks or predictability from pretraining loss.

Tests the effects of pretraining-data composition and two fitting approaches in this setup. It does not comprehensively test parameter-counting choices, training schedules, or other sources of published-law disagreement.
